subject: Psychiatry
summary: Post‑traumatic stress disorder is a psychiatric condition that develops after exposure to a traumatic event, marked by re‑experiencing, avoidance, and hyperarousal. It requires a structured interview and DSM‑5 criteria for diagnosis.

sections.p: PTSD is defined by DSM‑5 as a disorder following a traumatic event, with symptoms lasting >1 month and causing distress or impairment.
b: Traumatic event: threat to life, serious injury, or sexual violence

t.b: Confirms presence of core symptoms and duration

sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom count and functional impairment, using the Clinician‑Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS‑5) score ranges.
Primary causes are exposure to life‑threatening events; secondary causes include chronic stressors and comorbid medical conditions.

t.b: Can precipitate PTSD in low‑resource settings

sections.p: Patients report flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance of reminders, hypervigilance, and emotional numbing, often with sleep disturbance and concentration problems.
No laboratory test confirms PTSD, but investigations rule out medical mimics and assess comorbidities.

t.b: Excludes anemia or infection that may mimic fatigue
Rules out hepatic causes of mood changes
Identifies HIV, which can worsen PTSD

sections.p: Severe PTSD can lead to self‑harm, substance abuse, or suicide; chronic PTSD may cause cardiovascular disease and impaired cognition.
Treat the underlying trauma, provide psychotherapy, and use pharmacotherapy when indicated. Monitor for side effects and drug interactions.
b: Prazosin for nightmares (avoid in low‑resource settings if not available)

t.b: Treat core symptoms; avoid benzodiazepines due to dependence risk

sections.p: Regular review of symptom trajectory, medication adherence, and functional status. Prevention focuses on early intervention after trauma.
Differential includes acute stress reaction, adjustment disorder, depression, and generalized anxiety disorder.
Normal lab tests may mask underlying medical causes of mood changes; low‑resource settings may lack imaging for brain injury.
b: Normal EEG may miss subtle seizures

whenToSeekHelp: Uncontrolled hypertension or cardiac events related to hyperarousal

faq.q: Can PTSD develop after a single event?
faq.a: Yes, even one traumatic incident can trigger PTSD if symptoms persist >1 month.
Medication helps symptoms but therapy is essential for long‑term recovery.

faq.q: What if I cannot afford therapy?
faq.a: Support groups, community counseling, and low‑dose SSRIs are viable alternatives in low‑resource settings.

exam: Describe the DSM‑5 criteria for PTSD and explain how you would differentiate it from acute stress reaction.
Explain why SSRIs are preferred over benzodiazepines in PTSD management.
